food.text: When Polynesian seafarers reached the Hawaiian Islands between 1000 and 1200 AD, few edible plants grew there apart from ferns and some fruits found at higher elevations. Botanists and archaeologists believe the voyagers introduced between 27 and more than 30 plants, known as canoe plants, mainly for food.

Sweet potato, a South American plant, was cultivated by many Polynesian cultures before Western exploration, which is seen as evidence of contact with South America. It has been radiocarbon-dated in the Cook Islands to 1000 AD. Current thinking is that it reached central Polynesia around 700 AD and spread from there to Hawaii and New Zealand.
Ancient Hawaiian cuisine was sustained by diversified agroforestry and aquaculture. This is described in the article as the basis of Native Hawaiian cuisine in the period before European contact.

The most important of the canoe plants brought to Hawaii was taro. Native Hawaiians raised taro for poi, a smooth puree made from the taro corm, and also planted coconuts, sugarcane, sweet potatoes and yams. Pigs and dogs were killed by strangulation or by holding their nostrils shut, to conserve their blood. Chickens, pigs and dogs were then cooked in earth ovens with hot rocks inserted in their abdominal cavities.

Tahiti and the Marquesas are known for a unique food made by preserving breadfruit, called ma. It can be baked further in the earth oven, or eaten directly. In the Marquesas it is mixed with fresh breadfruit and eaten as popoi mei.

According to one account, by about 1000 the settlements founded along the perimeters of the Hawaiian Islands were beginning to cultivate their own foods in gardens. By 1500 they would begin to spread inward to the interiors of the islands.

Ti leaves were used as a wrapper for food cooked in the imu, the Hawaiian earth oven. Laulau, pieces of pork and salted black cod encased in taro and tī leaves, is one dish prepared this way; modern variations may use other proteins such as fish, chicken or beef.
Before the Polynesian settlers arrived, the Hawaiian Islands had few edible plants beyond ferns and high-elevation fruits. One fern, hāpuʻu ʻiʻi, has uncoiled fronds that are eaten boiled.

Hawaiian taro patches, called loʻi, were the Hawaiians' adaptation of paddy agriculture inherited from their Austronesian ancestors. Knowledge of the rice grain was gradually lost during the expansion into the Pacific. Rice cultivation later reused wet taro patches.

art.text: On Savai'i island in Samoa, the site of the Pulemelei mound, the largest ancient structure in the Samoan Islands, shows stronger evidence of human activity during the second half of the Samoan 'Dark Age,' between 700 and 1000 AD. This period predates the mound's main construction, which has been radiocarbon-dated to between 1100 and 1400 AD.

Beginning around 1100 AD, the people of Easter Island started building nearly 900 moai, which are large stone statues. This monumental sculpture is one of the best-known artistic achievements of the medieval Pacific.

At about 1200 AD, the people of Pohnpei, a Micronesian island, began building Nan Madol. It was a city of artificial islands linked by a system of canals, and it was a second great megalithic construction project of the medieval Pacific.

The noho aliʻi, the native rulers of the Hawaiian islands, were known for their brightly colored and intricately constructed battle regalia. It included feathered capes called ʻahu ʻula and feathered helmets called mahiole. A single ʻahu ʻula took thousands of birds to supply its feathers.
Beginning around 1100 CE, the people of Easter Island began building nearly 900 moai, which are large stone statues. It was a huge undertaking for a small, remote island.

The large stone statues of Easter Island, the moai, were carved between 1100 and 1680 CE, according to rectified radio-carbon dates. A total of 887 monolithic statues have been inventoried on the island and in museum collections.

Hawaiian aliʻi had specific items, tokens and other regalia that identified them as divine, powerful, high ranking and wealthy. Many of these items were status symbols because of their rarity, high value or magnificence.

Micronesian rock art traditions can be divided into western, central, and eastern regions. The eastern tradition reflects a back-migration from western Polynesia into eastern Micronesia around 1,000 BP.
By 1500 the first European explorers began to reach Oceania. Earlier artistic and architectural traditions continued, but the various regions began to diverge and record more distinct cultures.

war.text: The Tuʻi Tonga Empire built Tongan hegemony across Oceania through expansion beginning around 950 CE, peaking between 1200 and 1500. It was centered on the island of Tongatapu, with its capital at Muʻa.

The empire's dominance rested largely on its Imperial Navy, whose long-distance double canoes carried triangular sails across the Pacific. The largest kalia-type canoes could hold up to 100 men, giving Tonga the naval strength to command tribute and trade throughout the region.

The strength of the Tongan navy allowed the empire's reach to extend as far as the Tuvaluan archipelago. The oral history of Nanumea, one of Tuvalu's islands, traces its founding ancestor back to Tonga.

Fiji lay within the sphere of influence of the Tuʻi Tonga Empire, established in the 10th century, which brought Tongan and Polynesian customs and language into Fijian society. This empire began to decline in the 13th century.
Tongan expansion did not always succeed. Oral history from Niutao recalls that in the 15th century, Tongan warriors were defeated in a battle fought on the island's reef.

Among the Tongan navy's most famous vessels were the Tongafuesia, the ʻĀkiheuho, and the great warship Lomipeau. Another, the Takaʻipōmana, was actually a Samoan kalia that had once carried the bride Tohuʻia Limapō from Samoa to wed the Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua.
Tongan warriors invaded Niutao again later in the 15th century. They were repelled once more, according to Niutao's oral history.

literature.text: On Easter Island, a system of carved glyphs called rongorongo has the appearance of writing, though no one has ever fully deciphered it. Oral tradition says that only a small elite of ruling families and priests were ever able to read the sacred tablets. Early visitors were told that these ruling families and priests were all kidnapped in the Peruvian slaving raids or died soon afterward in the resulting epidemics, and by the 1870s few if any of the Rapanui remaining on the island could read the glyphs.

Tahiti was settled by Polynesians between 900 and 1100 CE. Tahitian culture included an oral tradition centered on the mythology of gods such as ʻOro, along with ancient traditions such as tattooing and navigation.

Two dozen wooden objects inscribed with rongorongo symbols have survived, including tablets, a chieftain's staff, a tangata manu statuette, and two reimiro ornaments. None of these objects remain on Easter Island itself; all were collected by outsiders in the nineteenth century and are now scattered in museums and private collections.

Polynesian history was passed down through oral genealogy chants recited at formal and family functions. The genealogy of high chiefs could be traced back to a time believed to be inhabited by gods, and the pua ali'i were considered living gods.

The clearing of forest for agriculture on Easter Island has been dated to around 1200, marking the likely start of settlement there. Since rongorongo could only have been invented after people arrived, this suggests the script is no older than the 13th century.

Many of the surviving rongorongo tablets were carved from whatever wood was on hand, including driftwood, rather than timber chosen specially for the purpose. By the time they were collected, some were already heavily weathered, burned, or otherwise damaged.

One rongorongo tablet, now kept in Rome, was carbon dated in a study published in 2024 and found to date to the mid-15th century, suggesting rongorongo may have been in use well before Europeans reached Easter Island.

Authentic rongorongo texts are carved in alternating directions, a technique known as reverse boustrophedon. In about a third of the surviving tablets, the lines of text sit within shallow grooves cut into the wood.

Oral tradition on Easter Island credits the legendary founder Hotu Matuʻa, or alternatively Tuʻu ko Iho, with bringing 67 rongorongo tablets from a distant homeland. Yet no likely homeland is known to have had its own tradition of writing, in Polynesia or even in South America, suggesting rongorongo was invented locally.

science.text: The first Tahitians arrived in the Society Islands from Western Polynesia sometime after 900 CE. They traveled in outrigger canoes up to twenty or thirty metres long, large enough to carry families as well as domestic animals.

The first Tahitians likely arrived from western Polynesia sometime after 900 CE, with some studies suggesting dates as late as 1025 to 1120 CE. They travelled aboard outrigger canoes up to twenty or thirty metres long, capable of carrying whole families along with domestic animals.
Navigators of Austronesian origin were the first to reach Micronesia and Polynesia. Perhaps a millennium ago, they even reached South America.

Linguistic, biological and archaeological evidence supports a long migration to Tahiti from Southeast Asia, passing through the Fijian, Samoan and Tongan Archipelagos. Some studies propose settlement dates slightly later than 900 CE, around 1025 to 1120 CE.

politics.text: The Tuʻi Tonga Empire describes Tongan expansionism and projected hegemony in Oceania that began around 950 CE. It reached its peak between 1200 and 1500. It was centred on the island of Tongatapu, with its capital at Muʻa.

In ancient Hawaii, a caste system established around 1200 AD separated the people into distinct ranks, all below the supreme ruler, the aliʻi nui. The aliʻi nui distributed land to lower ranking chiefs, who ran it and collected offerings and taxes.

The success of the Tongan Empire was largely based upon its Imperial Navy. The most common vessels were long-distance double-canoes with triangular sails. This large navy let Tonga grow wealthy as trade and tribute flowed into the royal treasury.

Tongan voyaging under the empire extended as far as the Tuvaluan archipelago. Niutao's oral history recalls that in the 15th century Tongan warriors were defeated in a battle on the reef. They invaded again later that century and were repelled once more.

In the 15th century Tongan society divided into two moieties, separated by the old coastal road Hala Fonua moa. Chiefs who derive authority from the Tuʻi Tonga are still called the Kau Hala ʻUta, or inland road people. Those from the Tuʻi Kanokupolu are the Kau Hala Lalo, or low road people.

A Tahitian priest named Pāʻao is said to have brought a new order to Hawaii around 1200, with new laws and a new social structure. The aliʻi nui was king, with his ʻaha kuhina just below. Next came the aliʻi nobles, the kahuna priests, the makaʻāinana commoners, and finally the kauā as the lowest caste.

Around 1200, a Tahitian priest named Pāʻao is said to have brought a new order to Hawaii that separated people into classes. The aliʻi nui was the king, and only the highest-ranking chiefs had the right to wear feathered regalia like the mahiole and ʻahu ʻula, representing their divinity and power.
The largest Tongan canoes of the kalia type could carry up to 100 men. Notable examples included the Tongafuesia, ʻĀkiheuho, Lomipeau and Takaʻipōmana. The Takaʻipōmana was actually a Samoan kalia.

Tohuʻia, a noblewoman from Safata, ʻUpolu, was the mother of the first Tuʻi Kanokupolu, Ngata. The Tupou line is considered to derive matrilineally from Samoa. Its crown jewels include fine mats such as the Maneafaingaa and Tasiaeafe.

The aliʻi nui were ultimately responsible for the sacred kapu, a strict code of conduct relating to taboos that was designed to control social order. It had rules covering many aspects of Hawaiian life, including fishing rights and even where women could eat. After the death of Kamehameha I the system was abolished, and the Hawaiian religion was also banned as Hawaiʻi was forcefully assimilated.

According to Queen Sālote and the Palace Records, the Samoan double-hulled canoe Takaʻipōmana brought Tohuʻia Limapō from Samoa to wed the Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua. Chiefly marriages with Samoan noblewomen were a route by which fine mats reached Tongan royal families.
Supporters of the Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua were Kauhalalalo when the division arose in the 15th century. Once the Tuʻi Kanokupolu had overtaken them, they shifted their allegiance to the Kauhalaʻuta.

Hawaiian rulers passed on their history through oral genealogy chants recited at formal and family functions. The genealogy of the high chiefs could be traced back to a period believed to be inhabited by gods. The pua aliʻi were considered to be living gods.

philosophy.text: Around 1200 AD, Pāʻao, a priest or chief from Tahiti, is thought to have arrived in Hawaiʻi bringing the kapu, a system of taboos separating the spiritually pure from the potentially unclean. It imposed restrictions on daily life: men and women had to eat apart (ʻaikapu), women were separated from the community while menstruating, and women were forbidden to eat pig, coconut, banana and certain red foods. Breaking the kapu could be punished by death, unless the offender escaped to a puʻuhonua, a city of refuge. Kāhuna nui also ordered long periods of absolute silence in a village, when no baby could cry, dog howl or rooster crow, on pain of death.

Between 1250 and 1500, the Rapa Nui people of Easter Island carved massive stone moai, whose size was linked to the mana, or spiritual power, of the chief who commissioned them. The moai served as the living faces of deified ancestors.

Early Hawaiians worshiped four major gods who embodied the forces of nature. Kāne ruled the sky and creation, Kū presided over war and male pursuits, Lono governed peace, rain, and fertility, and Kanaloa ruled the ocean.

The Polynesian concept of tapu, meaning sacred or forbidden, structured religious and social life across the Pacific, appearing among the Māori, Samoan, Tahitian, Hawaiian, Tongan, and Rapanui peoples under closely related names. It marked people, places, and objects as spiritually restricted. Among the Māori, burial grounds and places of death were always tapu and were often fenced off, and anyone ill or dying was moved to a shelter separate from the house. A violation of tapu could bring death to the offender, through sickness or at the hands of someone affected by the offence.

Within the kapu system, Hawaiians recognized the kahuna, an expert who held authority within Hawaiian religion. Kapu was a system of taboos meant to separate the spiritually pure from the potentially unclean. Punishments for breaking the kapu could include death, though someone who escaped to a puʻuhonua, a city of refuge, could be saved. Kāhuna nui mandated long periods of absolute silence in a village, and no baby could cry, dog howl or rooster crow, on pain of death.

The size of a moai reflected the mana, or spiritual power, of the chief who commissioned it, so the larger the statue placed on its ahu, the greater the chief's prestige. This fueled fierce competition among Rapa Nui clans to carve ever grander statues.

Across Polynesia, sacred communal grounds called marae, known as ahu on Easter Island, were cleared and bordered spaces used for religious ceremonies. In tropical Polynesia, most marae were destroyed or abandoned with the arrival of Christianity in the 19th century, and some have become attractions for tourists or archaeologists. Even so, the land where they once stood is still considered tapu, sacred or forbidden, in most of these cultures.

Nearly half of all moai remain at the Rano Raraku quarry where they were carved. Hundreds of others were transported across Easter Island and raised on ahu platforms as the living faces of deified ancestors.

In Hawaiian traditions the first man, Kumuhonua, was made by Kāne, or by Kāne, Kū, and Lono. His body was shaped from red earth mixed with saliva, and a woman was later made from one of his ribs. Kanaloa watched Kāne make him and made a man of his own, but could not bring him to life. Kanaloa then said to Kāne, "I will take your man, and he will die." And so death came upon humankind.

culture.text: Beginning around 1100 CE, the people of Easter Island began building nearly 900 moai, large stone statues. It was one of the great monument-building efforts of the Pacific in this era.
Around 1200 CE, the people of Pohnpei, a Micronesian island, began another megalithic project. They built Nan Madol, a city of artificial islands linked by a system of canals.

Polynesian navigators steered by the sun and stars and by watching cloud reflections and bird flight to find islands. A star or constellation used as a steering mark was called a kaweinga. By about 1280 AD, these voyagers had settled the whole Polynesian triangle, from Hawaii to Rapa Nui to New Zealand.

Ancient Hawaiian society was organized into ranks below the supreme ruler, the ali'i nui, in a caste system established around 1200 AD. A Tahitian priest named Pa'ao is said to have brought this new order, with new laws and social classes.

Easter Islanders claimed that a chief named Hotu Matu'a discovered their island in one or two large canoes, with his wife and extended family. Radiocarbon dates from charcoal, likely produced by forest clearance, suggest settlement as recently as 1200.
In the Hawaiian order, the ali'i were royal nobles, with priests called kahuna below them. Next came the commoners, the maka'ainana, and the kaua were the lowest social caste.
Entire small villages, called vanua, set sail together on great single and double-hulled canoes to discover new islands. Some voyages went against the prevailing winds and tides.
The ali'i nui were responsible for making sure people observed the kapu, a strict code of conduct relating to taboos. Its rules covered social order, fishing rights, and even where women could eat.

Ancient Hawaiian society was ruled under a strict kapu system, a code of conduct relating to taboos. Its rules covered many aspects of social order, including fishing rights and even where women could eat.

Radiocarbon evidence suggests Rapa Nui was settled by Polynesian voyagers around 1200 CE. Soon afterward, its people began major cultural investments in monumental architecture and statuary, alongside significant ecological changes to the island.

Chicken bones found by Chilean archaeologists on the Arauco Peninsula were thought to date from between 1321 and 1407 AD. This initial report suggested Polynesians had reached South America before Columbus, though a later report on the same specimens reached a different conclusion.

The noho ali'i were known for brightly colored, intricately made battle regalia. This included feathered capes called 'ahu 'ula and helmets called mahiole, worn only by the highest ranking chiefs. A single 'ahu 'ula took thousands of birds to supply its feathers.
